Appropriately is an adverb of appropriate “suitable”; its adjective descends from appropriatus and proprius “one’s own”.
Appropriateness is the noun of appropriate “suitable”; the base comes through Latin appropriatus from proprius “own”.
Appropriation is from Late Latin appropriatio, action noun from appropriare “make one’s own”, from proprius.
Appropriator is a person who appropriates, from appropriate “take, allocate”; the base comes from Latin proprius “one’s own”.
Inappropriate is negative in- plus appropriate “suitable”, from Latin appropriatus and proprius; the negative applies to suitability, not ownership.
Inappropriately is the listed adverb of inappropriate (in- plus appropriate), whose adjective base traces to proprius.
Inappropriateness is the listed noun of inappropriate, itself in- plus appropriate and historically proprius; the noun is the absence of suitability.
Misappropriate denotes wrongful appropriation, from mis- plus appropriate “take or assign”; the ownership stem is proprius.
Misappropriation is the dictionary-listed noun of misappropriate, whose base appropriate comes from Latin proprius.
Proprietorship is derived from proprietor; proprietor is from proprietary, ultimately Latin proprietarius/proprius “one’s own”.
Proprietress is proprietor plus -ess, with loss of the vowel in the suffixation; proprietor through proprietary descends from Latin proprius.
Reappropriation is the act of reappropriating, re- plus appropriate; the latter ultimately descends from Latin proprius.

MW explicitly lists parasit- as a combining form meaning parasite; independent Borror lists exact parasit and the parasite sense. Cambridge directly verifies parasitic both for living organisms and figuratively for people who take from others. This is a general figurative use in addition to basic school biology; BAWF Zipf 3.2157 is only a frequency hint. Etymonline traces parasitic through Latin parasiticus to Greek parasitikos, derivative of parasitos: parasit- is an indexed combining stem in the historical shape, not a claim that English newly coined it by attaching -ic to the modern written form parasit-. Dictionary.com explicitly points to parasite and -ic, an alternative modern analysis with silent-e removal. Keep both analyses and do not describe the individual modern meaning as food or grain. Independent cross-review: Merriam-Webster explicitly lists the full initial combining form parasit- meaning parasite, but its listed examples are not parasitic. An independent source directly connects the exact word to the exact longer stem: Danner, A Thesaurus of English Word Roots, parasit entry, classifies parasitic under SIMPLE ROOT. This is support for a synchronic teaching/indexing analysis of parasit-, not proof that an English speaker coined parasitic by adding -ic to the independent modern written form parasit. Dictionary.com explicitly traces the full word via Latin parasiticus and Greek parasitikos, followed by cross references to parasite and -ic; the latter are not by themselves a claim of an English coinage. Etymonline confirms the same borrowing chain. Merriam-Webster separately documents the ordinary figurative meaning of exploiting others as well as biological parasitism, so the general-language interpretation is sound. Its first attested figurative and later biological sense should not be described as necessarily a borrowing of the modern biological sense into figurative usage: Etymonline dates parasitic in the social sense before the biological sense. The component's direct meaning remains parasite, not literal food or grain. Danner also groups ectoparasite and endoparasite under parasit as prefixed roots. These compounds contain a complete parasite base after an initial prefix and show why a historical-root index should not enforce a whole-word-initial occurrence only. The MW source describes an initial combining form; recommend class root if the schema uses prefix to impose a strictly word-initial restriction, or retain prefix only with an explicit non-exclusive indexing rule. Do not erase the MW source's own position notation.
